episodes.159395: Several waterspouts were reported over the Chesapeake Bay in the morning, with localized gusty winds over the upper tidal Potomac River in the evening.
episodes.159529: As the month ended, high pressure was set to relocate to the western states and away from Arkansas. This allowed one last cold front to slide this way from the north. During the evening of the 31st, scattered thunderstorms formed near the Missouri border close to the front.||One storm became severe, and produced winds strong enough to destroy a metal carport and topple trees. This was far from the pounding (from damaging wind/isolated tornadoes) states to the north/east endured in recent days.
episodes.159549: Unusually moist airmass associated with a monsoon surge produce widespread thunderstorms. Flash flooding and debris flows occurred as a result, including on very recent burn scars.
episodes.159550: Unusually moist airmass associated with a monsoon surge produce widespread thunderstorms. Flash flooding and debris flows occurred as a result, including on very recent burn scars.
episodes.159702: A line of showers and storms that developed ahead of an approaching cold front crossed central Pennsylvania during the late-afternoon and early evening of August 1, 2021. In spite of relatively modest CAPE and shear, a couple of these storms were able to produce isolated wind damage.
episodes.159711: High pressure retrograted in response to a deepening mid-level trough over the center of the nation and parked over western Colorado. Even so, subtropical moisture remained entrenched over the area with precipitable water values exceeding an inch and trending over 150% of the climatological norm. As a result, widespread showers and thunderstorms erupted over western Colorado. Additionally, convergence along the Continental Divide enhanced storm coverage. Heavy rain and training was common with storms which led to numerous reports of flash flooding and debris flows, including over the Pine Gulch and Grizzly Creek Fire burn scars.
episodes.159861: A severe thunderstorm brought large hail to western Arkansas.
episodes.160301: Multiple locations experienced heavy rain, flooding, and debris flows due to slow-moving training storms.
episodes.160325: During the late afternoon of the 31st of July, several small thunderstorms developed with daytime heating as the summer monsoon moisture plume extended across the area. By evening, the initial storms sent out several outflow boundaries which collided with one another and created larger and stronger thunderstorms. While lack of wind shear (stronger winds aloft) caused these storms to collapse on themselves, the environment was favorable for collapsing storms to produce damaging wind gusts across the Texas Panhandle. Though no damage was reported several automated weather stations recorded wind gusts in excess of 60 mph.
episodes.160328: Early in the morning of the first, a slow moving cold front enhanced by convective outflow boundaries produced scattered thunderstorms across the South Plains and Rolling Plains. One of these storms moved directly over the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near O'Donnell generating a severe wind gust.
episodes.160525: Thunderstorms along a weak cold front sinking south into central Georgia produced isolated reports of damaging thunderstorm winds.
episodes.160658: A single storm intensified overnight and moved east across Monroe County, producing wind gusts that blew down trees.
episodes.161115: SW flow focused afternoon and evening sea breeze storms toward the Atlantic coast. A weak surface front was draped across NE FL which aided in convergence.
episodes.161228: An isolated severe storm produced wind damage.
episodes.161229: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed along and south of a cold front which moved from north to south across the region during the afternoon into early evening. Reports of wind damage to trees were received from Joplin to Mount Vernon to Springfield and southeastward to near Gainesville. Rainfall accumulations averaged between one-half inch and one inch, with isolated accumulations over two inches near Rolla and Camdenton.
episodes.161315: Sustained monsoonal flow brought more flooding to southeast Idaho on July 31st.
episodes.161377: An active monsoon surge brought several back-to-back days of thunderstorms producing heavy rain, damaging wind gusts, and hail across the state.
episodes.161585: A severe thunderstorm moved across Sumner and Sedgwick counties during the evening hours.
episodes.161616: After a brief break, another push of monsoon moisture fueled another round of thunderstorms over the Mojave Desert. Some storms produced flash flooding.
episodes.161652: A surface low moved from northern Lake Huron during the predawn hours of the 1st to eastern Lake Ontario by early afternoon. This allowed the trailing cold front to sweep southeastward across Lake Erie during the midmorning through late morning hours. Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms developed amidst weak to moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear along and ahead of the front. Some of the cells were accompanied by waterspouts. Horizontal wind shear along the cold front and downshear gust fronts generated surface-based vertical vorticity. In turn, the waterspouts likely formed as updrafts ingested the surface-based vertical vorticity and stretched it to greater strength.
episodes.161687: Scattered showers and thunderstorms, including some supercells, developed across Middle Tennessee during the evening hours on July 31 and moved southeastward. Numerous reports of damaging winds and flash flooding were received.
episodes.161760: A cold front pushed into northern sections of the Mid-South during the late evening hours of July 31, 2021.  The front intersected a hot and humid airmass and storms erupted along the front. Storms pushed south producing scattered wind damage mainly along and north of Interstate 40.
episodes.161771: Monsoonal subtropical moisture set the stage for thunderstorms to produce heavy rainfall across portions of the central Idaho.
episodes.161781: A cold front pushed into northern sections of the Mid-South during the late evening hours of July 31, 2021. The front intersected a hot and humid airmass and storms erupted along the front. Storms pushed south producing scattered wind damage mainly along and north of Interstate 40.
episodes.161878: Isolated storms developed along an outflow boundary across south central portions of the CWA through the tail end of the frontal boundary coupled with weak upslope flow off the Ration Mesa. Deep level shear was relatively weak but with the hot temperatures, instability was enough to support isolated storms with damaging wind gusts associated with downbursts the main threat.
episodes.161905: Continued push of monsoonal moisture into Idaho caused continued flooding into the first couple of days of August.
episodes.161950: The combination of the monsoon plume and moist low level upslope flow allowed for thunderstorms with heavy rainfall and flash flooding to occur on this day across the region. The highest concern for flash flooding was over the mountains and I-25 corridor region, but later in the evening, additional flash flooding occurred along and south of Highway 50.
episodes.162007: An environment marked by warm and moist conditions favored strong to severe thunderstorms near a stationary front while a wave of mid-level energy traveled across the southeast Georgia.
episodes.162032: A line of showers and thunderstorms pushed across eastern New York on Sunday, August 1, 2021. One of the thunderstorms became severe, downing a tree in the City of Johnstown.
episodes.162056: A line of strong to briefly severe storms moved across portions of southwest Georgia on the afternoon of August 1st with several reports of trees and power lines blown down.
episodes.162123: A band of thunderstorms dropped southeast from middle Tennessee into southern middle Tennessee just before Midnight. Strong winds along the gust front knocked down several trees in Fayetteville in Lincoln County, and a couple of trees in Sewanee in Franklin County.
episodes.162136: A line of storms developed ahead of a passing cold front. With moisture and instability present, a couple of storms became severe, knocking down a few trees across Central New York.
episodes.162138: A line of storms developed ahead of a passing cold front. With moisture and instability present, one storm became severe, knocking down a few trees across in Luzerne County in Northeastern Pennsylvania.

episodes.162185: Strong thunderstorms were associated with a stalled boundary.
episodes.162212: Scattered thunderstorms along a frontal boundary produced a waterspout across portions of the Currituck Sound.
episodes.162215: Scattered thunderstorms along a frontal boundary produced gusty winds across portions of the Currituck Sound and the northeast North Carolina Coastal Waters.
episodes.162217: Scattered severe thunderstorms along a frontal boundary produced damaging winds and one weak tornado across portions of northeast North Carolina.
episodes.162220: Scattered thunderstorms along a frontal boundary produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of southeast Virginia.
episodes.162268: Thunderstorms developed along a rare August cold front as it pushed south into North and Central Texas on the afternoon and evening of Sunday August 1. A few storms produce severe hail and gusty winds. Frequent lightning also damaged multiple homes.
episodes.162270: A cold front moved into a warm, moist airmass and generated thunderstorms over South Central Texas. Some of these storms produced locally heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
episodes.162438: Widespread moderate to heavy rainfall occurred across much of the eastern mountains and adjacent locations along the I-25 corridor on this day. Rainfall as high as 2 to 5 inches was observed in many locations, with flash flooding occurring across parts of Pueblo county.
episodes.162572: Showers and thunderstorms developed during the early to mid afternoon along a stationary front draped across central North Carolina from northeast to southwest. A very moist and unstable airmass was in place south of the stationary front. This combined with an unseasonably strong mid/upper level trough over the are resulted in a deep layer shear profile favorable for multicellular clusters and even a few supercells. Thus, as the showers and storms developed they quickly developed into clusters of storms with embedded supercells. Multiple storms/clusters became severe and produced wind damaging and large hail.
episodes.162584: A thunderstorm moved over northern Lake Huron during the early morning hours and produced wind gusts in excess of 40 mph over the open waters.
episodes.162616: An active monsoon surge brought thunderstorms producing heavy rain, damaging wind gusts, and hail across the state.
episodes.162629: Deep moisture over northern Arizona lead to scattered thunderstorms with heavy rain that caused flash flooding.
episodes.162632: Thunderstorms developed across the foothills during the early morning along a stationary front and moved into the northwest Piedmont. One of these storms produced damaging wind gusts and large hail in Iredell and Davie Counties.
episodes.162757: A digging and sharpening mid-level trough moved from the central Great Lakes in the morning to the eastern Great Lakes by early evening. At the surface, a cold front and weak frontal wave crossed the eastern Great Lakes. Shear was marginally supportive of severe weather with about 25 knots of effective shear. Extensive clouds and showers hampered destabilization across the bulk of the area. Some breaks in the rain and dense overcast allowed for a little greater instability to develop near the Pennsylvania state line, and this supported a broken line of thunderstorms around midday.|Most of the storms were only producing heavy rain and frequent lightning. Later in the day, under the sharpening trough and upper level low, showers and thunderstorms blossomed over the Great Lakes. Cold air aloft associated with the low allowed for temperatures to fall at 850 hPa low enough to support waterspout formation.
episodes.162758: A digging and sharpening mid-level trough moved from the central Great Lakes in the morning to the eastern Great Lakes by early evening. episodes.162762: An area of low pressure moved northeast of North Carolina, with a weak trailing cold front moving across Eastern North Carolina.  Ahead of this front, a broken line of thunderstorms developed, some of which produced wind damage.
episodes.162789: Monsoonal moisture associated with a low pressure system brought locally heavy rain and thunderstorms to southwestern Oregon and southeastern Idaho. Flash flood watches were issued to the area due to the extensive precipitation.

Widespread flash flooding occurred in Enoch and Cedar City, with up to 300 homes damaged by flood waters.  Water rescues were performed, and cars were swept off the road.  Interstate 15 was closed during the event.  Numerous roads were eroded by floodwaters, and Fiddlers Canyon was reported underwater.
ASOS recorded 0.85 inches of rain in 34 minutes.

Salmon-Challis National Forest officials reported a 30 feet wide by three feet deep sand and dirt debris flow across Salmon River Road, 1.5 miles west of Panther Creek. Another debris flow was reported from the Dutch Oven Creek drainage and was three feet wide, by four feet deep, including two to three boulders. The Salmon River Road was impassable from Panther Creek to Dutch Oven Creek through the morning hours of August 2nd. The Skull Gulch RAWS, located a few miles northwest of Panther Creek, reported 0.24 inches of rain from 1500 to 1600.

A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph near Fair Oaks Ranch. There were large tree branches reported down in the Balcones Creek Estates neighborhood.

At least 15 different debris flows were caused by previous thunderstorms/heavy rain during the afternoon. Multiple reports came from the US Forest Service, Elko County Road Department, and Nevada Department of Transportation. USFS 660 will be closed until further notice. The height of debris flows is estimated to be between 4 and 8 feet within a 4-mile length of road.
